overview: Rabies is a vaccine-preventable, zoonotic, viral disease affecting the central nervous system. It is a serious public health problem in over 150 countries and territories, mainly in Asia and Africa. Rabies is fatal in 100% of cases if not treated promptly after exposure.
symptoms: Aerophobia (fear of drafts or of fresh air)
diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on symptoms and history of contact with a rabid animal
Postmortem confirmation of rabies infection through laboratory techniques
treatment: Prompt post exposure prophylaxis (PEP) through thorough wound washing
Administration of a course of human rabies vaccine
Comprehensive and compassionate palliative care once symptoms emerge
transmission: Consumption of raw meat or milk of infected animals (rare)
Organ transplantation from an infected donor (rare)
prevention: Vaccinating dogs through mass dog vaccination programs
Public education on dog behaviour and bite prevention
Vaccinating people before and after potential exposures
risk_factors: People living in areas with high rabies incidence
People who engage in outdoor activities that increase the risk of animal bites
complications: Fatal inflammation of the brain and spinal cord
key_facts: Dog bites and scratches cause 99% of human rabies cases
The global cost of rabies is estimated to be around US$ 8.6 billion per year
Over 29 million people worldwide receive human rabies vaccine annually
